skills.name: Tools of analysis: variables, tables and relationships

note.text: Economists organise information using words, tables, diagrams and simple calculations. A variable can take different values, such as quantity sold. A table places observations in labelled rows and columns. Units identify what the values measure. A relationship describes how variables are associated. Association alone does not prove that one variable caused another to change: other influences may matter. Read the title, labels and units before using any values.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: Economists organise information using words, tables, diagrams and simple calculations. A variable can take different values, such as quantity sold. A table places observations in labelled rows and columns. Units identify what the values measure. A relationship describes how variables are associated. Association alone does not prove that one variable caused another to change: other influences may matter. Read the title, labels and units before using any values.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: A Bamenda trader records baskets of tomatoes sold on market days. A column headed baskets measures quantity, not CFA francs. A second column may record price per basket. Clear labels prevent a learner from adding a price to a quantity as though they measured the same thing. A record of higher sales on sunny days suggests a relationship to investigate, not proof that sunshine alone caused sales.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Name the variable and its unit. Read across the same row when comparing an observation. Keep price per item separate from total expenditure. When drawing a conclusion, say exactly which relationship the data show and which possible causes have not been checked.

key_words.meaning: a quantity or characteristic that can take different values
information arranged in labelled rows and columns
the measure in which a value is expressed

examples: The number of baskets sold changes from market day to market day.
A trader records each market day beside its quantity sold.
A heading says the price is in CFA francs per basket.

wrong.text: A variable must have the same value in every observation.
wrong.explain: It is called a variable because different values are possible.

wrong.text: An unlabelled list always identifies the meaning of its values.
wrong.explain: Rows, columns and headings are needed to make a table interpretable.

wrong.text: A price per basket is measured in baskets alone.

wrong.text: Every association proves a direct cause.
wrong.explain: Other factors may explain a relationship; association alone does not establish causation.
